questions.q: Which veins are most commonly involved in clinically significant lower-extremity deep vein thrombosis?
options: Posterior tibial and peroneal veins only
questions.explanation: Proximal DVT most commonly involves the femoral, popliteal, and iliac veins and carries the highest risk of pulmonary embolism. Superficial veins such as the great and small saphenous veins are not classified as deep veins.
questions.pearl: Proximal DVT is associated with a substantially higher risk of pulmonary embolism than isolated distal calf DVT.

questions.q: Virchow's triad consists of which three major contributors to venous thrombosis?
options: Hypercoagulability, venous stasis, and endothelial injury
questions.explanation: Virchow's triad describes the three principal mechanisms underlying thrombus formation: venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability.
questions.pearl: Most patients have multiple risk factors acting simultaneously.

questions.q: Which symptom is most commonly associated with acute lower-extremity DVT?
questions.explanation: The most common presentation is unilateral leg swelling with pain or tenderness. Some patients, however, may be asymptomatic.
questions.pearl: Clinical findings alone cannot reliably diagnose or exclude DVT.

questions.q: Which physical examination finding is considered most suggestive of DVT?
options: Localized calf tenderness with unilateral swelling
questions.explanation: Calf tenderness combined with unilateral swelling increases clinical suspicion, although physical examination alone lacks sufficient diagnostic accuracy.
questions.pearl: Clinical prediction tools such as the Wells score improve diagnostic assessment.

questions.q: What is the first-line imaging study for suspected lower-extremity DVT?
questions.explanation: Compression duplex ultrasound is the preferred initial imaging modality because it is accurate, noninvasive, and widely available.
questions.pearl: Failure of the vein to fully compress is the hallmark sonographic finding of DVT.

questions.q: Which histologic component predominates in a venous thrombus?
options: Fibrin and trapped red blood cells
questions.explanation: Venous thrombi are fibrin-rich ("red clots") that contain abundant erythrocytes trapped within a fibrin mesh.
questions.pearl: Venous thrombi differ from arterial thrombi, which are relatively platelet-rich.

questions.q: What is the most serious complication of untreated DVT?
questions.explanation: Embolization of thrombus to the pulmonary arteries can result in life-threatening pulmonary embolism.
questions.pearl: Prompt anticoagulation markedly reduces the risk of embolization.

questions.q: Which medication class is recommended as first-line treatment for most patients with acute DVT?
questions.explanation: Current guidelines recommend DOACs for most patients with acute DVT because they are effective and have a favorable safety profile.
questions.pearl: Treatment duration depends on whether the DVT is provoked or unprovoked.

questions.q: Which patient has the greatest risk for developing DVT?
options: Recent major orthopedic surgery with prolonged immobilization
questions.explanation: Major surgery, especially orthopedic procedures combined with immobilization, is one of the strongest acquired risk factors.
questions.pearl: Early ambulation and pharmacologic prophylaxis reduce postoperative DVT risk.

questions.q: Which statement best summarizes modern DVT management?
options: Early diagnosis and anticoagulation prevent pulmonary embolism and long-term complications.
questions.explanation: Prompt diagnosis followed by appropriate anticoagulation remains the cornerstone of DVT management.
questions.pearl: Always evaluate for pulmonary embolism in patients with DVT who develop chest pain or dyspnea.
